item.title: The Courage to Question Our Own Certainty
item.description:
Relationships

The Courage to Question Our Own Certainty

Learning to suspend your initial judgement is a critical practice to master.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Our minds generate interpretations so quickly, we mistake our subjective perceptions for objective reality.
  • Questioning our assumptions can deepen mutual understanding and reveal perspectives we may have overlooked.
  • Thoughtful receptivity involves pausing, separating fact from interpretation, and engaging with curiosity.
  • Questioning our certainty does not require abandoning our convictions, but recognizing we may be mistaken.

There are a plethora of potentially polarizing issues these days in all aspects of our lives! It seems that we can hardly get a point of view on the table before a fellow conversationalist debunks our idea and discredits us along the way. Take your pick from a bushel full of igniting issues, whether it be global warming, wars, increasing the tax percentage for the very wealthy, or the strengths and weaknesses of our favorite political personalities; there will be no shortage of strong opinions. You can also be assured that before the full set of points of view are exposed or explored, one or more folks will have already decided what the correct point of view should be.

Our positioning and decisions on an issue seem like they happen in the blink of an eye. This instant judgement can create ill will, stress for us and the other, and can challenge or ruin long-standing relationships. Furthermore, it will likely lead to a suboptimal exploration and resolution of the salient points of view. The pivot that I would like to explore is realizing that although our interpretations and positions usually feel quite certain to us, they most likely do not represent the whole of the reality of that situation; they are a narrower, biased slice of the problem or solution.

Source: Arnab Das / Pexels

I would like to explore what can happen when we can loosen our grip on our story/point of view, and instead consider what might ensue if we instead question our own certainty. This, of course, would require slowing down enough to really listen first and then explore the fuller reality of the situation together; then, with skillful listening and openness to other ways of thinking, we can have a meaningful and civil dialogue.

Why does this matter so much now?

We seem to be experiencing a plethora of fractured conversations, competing accounts of the truth, information overload, and fear about the future, all of which are leading to what we might call “contemporary exhaustion.” And if the impact of this on us personally wasn’t enough, the relational tension as well as the societal and political challenges are at an all-time high. It is so much more likely that answers to our difficult questions will land somewhere in the middle of the two opposing extremes being debated, or in a yet-to-be-discovered “third alternative” idea that cannot possibly be uncovered because of the anger, tension, and lack of listening in the interchange. Just to ground this idea in one statistic: the American Psychological Association's Stress in America survey, "A Crisis of Connection," reported that 62% of adults considered societal divisions a significant stressor in their lives.

The practice of thoughtful receptivity

If you are willing to have the “courage to suspend the certainty” of your initial interpretation and allow for more information, thoughts, and feelings to emerge between you and another, amazing things can happen. Try following a simple practice of what I will call “thoughtful receptivity” using these 4 steps. Imagine that, before you know it, you are in a polarizing conversation with challenging points of view and heated feelings emerging. Each side draws his/her sword, and the point-counterpoint debate begins. You have enough presence to realize you are in the battle, and it likely will not end well. You feel triggered and notice the same for the other person. You remember this practice and do the following:

  1. Notice the physical impulse to defend, accuse, retreat, or judge. Press the pause button and take a deep breath to center yourself. This is the key to breaking the cycle, which takes some focus and consciousness, as our tendency is a knee-jerk reaction to engage in the “battle” in front of us.
  2. Separate from your tendency to react emotionally. Instead, see that there is an opportunity to engage more thoughtfully. Ask what the objective “fly on the wall” might see or hear if observing this conversation. Separate from your initial interpretation by staying in the “neo-cortex” part of the brain, which is more rational, and not succumbing to the amygdala, which is more reactive.
  3. Widen your perspective by generating other plausible interpretations of the issue besides the initial one you postulated. Ask yourself what the other person is really trying to say. Open to other ways of considering and answering questions and loosen the grip on your closely held opinion or hypothesis. (This step is very hard for sure.)
  4. Re-engage by asking one or more genuinely curious and open questions of the other. These generative questions are ones that you truly do not know the answer to currently. An example might be, “Tell me more about your thoughts.”

We all have the tendency to confuse the story we have crafted and are trying to tell with the whole truth about a situation. Perhaps a better way to proceed is to remain open to what we have not yet explored or understood, remain open to another way of thinking about a situation, and remain open to the other person. If we could find the grace to do so, we might learn to see and understand more deeply before we judge. All of this ultimately requires that we develop the courage to question our own certainty. If we could do so, it is very likely that our world would become a much better, kinder place to live and thrive.

item.title: 3 Things to Do When Your Adult Child Pulls Away
item.description:
Parenting

3 Things to Do When Your Adult Child Pulls Away

Whether you talk every once in a while or have not spoken in years, this helps.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • The better you name what you miss, the better you will know what to say.
  • A specific apology gives your adult child room to share their experience.
  • Respecting your child's wishes about contact is a great way to show you listened.

Just last week, my parent coaching client looked at me quizzically while describing a recent text from her son. The text was just a photo of her son's dog wearing (or at least trying to wear) a cap of a major league baseball team. She said, "Dr. Jeff, it's been two months since I last heard from him, and of course, I immediately smiled when I saw the pic. But I had no idea what to do next." This client elaborated that her fingers led her to compose and immediately delete five responses prior to sending them. She added, "No matter what I do, he will pull away again, anyway."

The Absence of Contact Has a Great Presence

The client above was struggling with how to respond after a long lag in communication with her adult child. She didn't know whether to joke about the cute picture, or tell her son she missed him, or ask further about Thanksgiving. For any parents in similar situations, it can be maddening to feel unsure about how to respond. And, if you have not spoken to your adult child for over six months or even years, the absence of that relationship has a huge, seemingly constant presence. By this I mean that often in these partial or full-on estrangement situations, the reality is that minimal or no contact does not take away from the internal emotional upheaval that comes from the desire to reconnect.

It is easy to feel helpless in the face of not seeing your adult child or not having the level of connection that you value. In my parent coaching work, I encourage parents to focus on three things they can do no matter how long it's been since they last heard their grown child's voice.

1. Name What You Miss to Help Manage It

Finish this sentence: "What I miss most about my grown child today is__________." Some parents might reply that they wish they knew how their son was doing. Maybe, as in the early example of the dog photo, a parent misses lighter moments of laughter. Maybe a song reminds you of your adult child.

Identifying what you miss is tangible and healthy because it helps you process difficult feelings like sadness, disappointment, nostalgia, or loneliness. For example, that treasured memory of you and your daughter going for a ride and belting out a shared favorite song may weigh heavily on your mind. Consider sharing these thoughts with trusted relatives, friends, a therapist, or a parent coach. Sometimes it helps to have someone just say, "Tell me more."

2. Own the Part You Wish You Did Differently

Consider your adult daughter saying to you, "When I tell you what bothered me that you did when I was growing up, you kept twisting it to make it my fault and giving me advice." You may remember trying to help. But hold on, because, at the same time, maybe you can recall trying to give her advice when she said, "Dad, can I finish my point?"

Looking at your own behaviors in this way gives you an honest point of reflection to start. You could then say, "I've been reflecting on times I rushed in to give you advice, and it got in the way of better understanding what you were going through, and I'm sorry." This type of dialogue not only shows that you are taking responsibility, but you are also modeling self-awareness to your adult child.

In my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, I explore how easily a parent's regret can turn into a feeling of indebtedness. In the parent coaching trenches, I have seen how tempting it is for parents to promise their adult children something to bring them closer. Please keep in mind that you can offer a sincere apology and still take your time to decide what you can reasonably do or give. For parents who are totally out of contact, I suggest you write down what you regret and keep it private.

3. Respect Your Adult Child's Pace of Contact

This third point is really hard for parents missing their adult children. If several messages go unanswered, give your adult child room to reach out. If they asked for no contact, honor that request. Believe it or not, adult children in these situations often share with me that they still love and even miss their parents, even when they outwardly state they want no contact. Just remember what I wrote above: The absence of contact still has a great presence in both your mind and that of your adult child.
